signaling, and transport

ABSTRACT
Cytokinins are mobile phytohormones that regulate plant growth, development, and environmental adaptability. The major cytokinin species include isopentenyl adenine (iP), trans-zeatin (tZ), cis-zeatin (cZ), and
dihydrozeatin (DZ). The spatial distributions of different cytokinin species in different organelles, cells, tissues, and organs are primarily shaped by biosynthesis via isopentenyltransferases (IPT), cytochrome P450
monooxygenase, and 50
-ribonucleotide phosphohydrolase and by conjugation or catabolism via glycosyltransferase or cytokinin oxidase/dehydrogenase. Cytokinins bind to histidine receptor kinases in the endoplasmic reticulum or plasma membrane and relay signals to response regulators in the nucleus via shuttle
proteins known as histidine phosphotransfer proteins. The movements of cytokinins from sites of biosynthesis to sites of signal perception usually require long-distance, intercellular, and intracellular transport. In
the past decade, ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, purine permeases (PUP), AZA-GUANINE
RESISTANT (AZG) transporters, equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT), and Sugars Will Eventually

Be Exported transporters (SWEET) have been characterized as involved in cytokinin transport processes.
This review begins by introducing the spatial distributions of various cytokinins and the subcellular localizations of the proteins involved in their metabolism and signaling. Highlights focus on an inventory of the
characterized transporters involved in cytokinin compartmentalization, including long-distance, intercellular, and intracellular transport, and the regulation of the spatial distributions of cytokinins by environmental cues. Future directions for cytokinin research are also discussed.
Key words: cytokinin, biosynthesis, transporter, signal transduction, environmental changes

INTRODUCTION
Cytokinins were discovered in a search for factors that promote
cell proliferation in plant tissue culture alongside auxin (Miller,
1955a). In 1955, Miller and Skoog from the botany and
biochemistry departments at the University of Wisconsin
reported the isolation, crystallization, characterization, and
synthesis of kinetin (6-furfurylaminopurine) (Miller, 1955b). The
first isolation of trans-zeatin (tZ) in plants was from corn (Zea
mays) endosperm in 1961 (Miller, 1961). Subsequently, various
types of cytokinins, including N6
-(D2-isopentenyl)adenine (iP),
cis-zeatin (cZ), dihydrozeatin (DZ), and aromatic cytokinins,
were discovered and characterized (Sondheimer and Tzou,
1971; Horgan et al., 1973, 1975; Laloue et al., 1974, 1977;
Kaiss-Chapman and Morris, 1977; Wang and Horgan,
1978; Letham and Palni, 1983). The metabolism, signaling,
and transport of various types of cytokinins have been
comprehensively investigated over the past 70 years.
Cytokinin metabolic pathways have been well characterized. The

key enzymes involved in cytokinin metabolism are as follows: isopentenyltransferase (IPT) catalyzes the transfer of isopentenyl
groups to the adenine of ATP and ADP, thereby producing isopentenyladenine nucleotides; cytochrome P450 (CYP) monooxygenase enables hydroxylation of iP nucleotides to produce zeatin

biosynthesis, O- and N-glucosyltransferases are responsible for
cytokinin glucosylation, and cytokinin oxidase/dehydrogenases
(CKXs) are responsible for irreversible degradation of cytokinins
to mediate cytokinin homeostasis and signaling (Fox et al.,
1973; Letham et al., 1983; Bilyeu et al., 2001; Galuszka et al.,
2001; Werner et al., 2001; Veach et al., 2003; Hou et al., 2004;
Ashikari et al., 2005; Bartrina et al., 2011).
The cytokinin signaling system is composed of histidine (His) receptor kinases (HKs), His phosphotransfer proteins (HPs), and

response regulators (RRs) (Kiba et al., 1999; D’Agostino et al.,
2000; Sakakibara et al., 2000; Hwang and Sheen, 2001; Inoue
et al., 2001; Ueguchi et al., 2001a, 2001b; Yamada et al., 2001;
Hwang et al., 2002; Hwang et al., 2012). In brief, cytokinins
bind HKs, stimulating His phosphorylation and triggering a
phosphorelay that results in the transfer of phosphoryl groups
onto aspartate (Asp) residues of HKs. Subsequently, these
phosphoryl groups are further transferred onto His residues of
HPs. Finally, the HPs transfer the phosphoryl groups to the
conserved Asp of RR members via direct interaction, leading to
the activation of gene transcription (Sakakibara et al., 2000;
Hwang and Sheen, 2001; Inoue et al., 2001; Hwang et al.,
2012). Throughout these processes, HP proteins shuttle
between the cytoplasm and the nucleus to transfer activating
phosphoryl groups to the receiver domains of RRs, thus
facilitating the connection of endoplasmic reticulum (ER)- or
plasma membrane (PM)-localized receptors with nuclear RRs
(Sakakibara et al., 2000; Hwang and Sheen, 2001; Caesar et al.,
2011; Lomin et al., 2011; Wulfetange et al., 2011).
Cytokinin biosynthesis and signaling typically occur in different
organelles, cells, tissues, and organs. Cytokinin homeostasis
and signal perception rely on autocrine, paracrine, or longdistance translocation. Serving as a link between biosynthesis
and signaling, cytokinin transport plays essential roles in plant
development and responses to environmental cues. The
spatial distributions of multiple cytokinin species in different
organelles, cells, tissues, or organs require sophisticated
transport mechanisms. Comprehensive reviews of cytokinin
biosynthesis, signaling, or transport have been published previously (Sakakibara, 2006, 2021; Hwang et al., 2012; Zurcher €

and Muller, 2016 € ; Liu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023). Here,
we review recent progress in the study of cytokinin transport
and the regulation of the spatial distributions of cytokinin
species, metabolic enzymes, and signaling components.
CYTOKININ BIOSYNTHESIS
Biosynthesis of iP-, tZ-, and cZ-type cytokinin
nucleotides in the plastids, cytoplasm, and ER
Cytokinins are a class of N6-adenine derivatives that can be
divided into isoprenoid and aromatic cytokinins on the basis of
side-chain structure (Miller, 1961; Horgan et al., 1973, 1975;
Mok, 1994; Strnad, 1997). Isoprenoid cytokinins are widely
present in plants, and their synthesis and metabolism have
been studied extensively. Isoprenoid cytokinins mainly include
iP-, tZ-, cZ-, and DZ-type cytokinins (Mok and Mok, 2001). The
initiation step of isoprenoid cytokinin biosynthesis is catalyzed
by IPTs, which are classified into three types: ATP/ADP-IPT,
AMP-IPT, and tRNA-IPT (Kakimoto, 2001; Takei et al., 2001;
Miyawaki et al., 2006; Matsumoto-Kitano et al., 2008; KamadaNobusada and Sakakibara, 2009; Frebort et al., 2011; Wang
et al., 2020). ATP/ADP-IPT is present mainly in plants, whereas
AMP-IPT is present mainly in bacteria and non-plant eukaryotes,
with tRNA-IPTs possessing a much broader taxonomic distribution (Kakimoto, 2001; Frebort et al., 2011; Ghosh et al., 2018;
Wang et al., 2020). In this review, we mainly focus on cytokinin
synthesis in plants (Figure 1). ATP/ADP-IPT catalyzes cytokinin

synthesis using dimethylallyl diphosphate and ATP/ADP as substrates to produce iP nucleotides, including iP riboside 50
-triphosphate (iPRTP) and iP riboside 50
-diphosphate (iPRDP) (Kakimoto,
2001; Takei et al., 2001, 2003). tRNA-IPT catalyzes the synthesis
of cis-hydroxy isopentenyl tRNAs, which are transformed into cZ
riboside 50
-monophosphate (Golovko et al., 2002; Miyawaki
et al., 2006).
Nine IPT genes (IPT1–9) have been annotated in the Arabidopsis
genome (Kakimoto, 2001; Takei et al., 2001; Miyawaki et al.,
2006). The AtIPT1 and AtIPT3–8 enzymes preferentially use ATP
and ADP as isoprenoid acceptors (Kakimoto, 2001; Takei et al.,
2001). AtIPT2 and AtIPT9 catalyze the isoprenylation of tRNA,
providing a source for cZ-type cytokinins (Miyawaki et al., 2006).
At subcellular levels, AtIPT2 and AtIPT4 localize to the cytoplasm,
AtIPT7 to mitochondria, and AtIPT1, AtIPT3, AtIPT5, and AtIPT8 to
plastids (Kasahara et al., 2004; Galichet et al., 2008). Dimethylallyl
diphosphate, another substrate of IPT, is produced from the
methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway in the plastids.
Experiments using 13C labeling have shown that iP- and tZ-type
cytokinins are mainly synthesized via the MEP pathway, which is
consistent with the localization of most ATP/ADP-IPT enzymes
(Kasahara et al., 2004). cZ-type cytokinins are synthesized by
both the MEP and mevalonate (MVA) pathways, but primarily via
the MVA pathway, consistent with the localization of IPT2 in the

cytoplasm (Kasahara et al., 2004). These data suggest that the
iPRTP/iPRDP/iPRMP for iP biosynthesis is mainly produced in
the plastids, whereas the cZ riboside 50
-monophosphate for cZ
biosynthesis is produced in the cytoplasm. The physiological
and biochemical functions of the IPT gene family have also
been characterized in species other than Arabidopsis, such as
Streptocarpus rexii and Jatropha curcas (Kamada-Nobusada
et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020).
CYP735A1 and A2 are two P450 enzymes responsible for the
side modification of iPRTP/iPRDP/iPRMP in plants such as
Arabidopsis and rice (Oryza sativa) (Takei et al., 2004a).
Although the subcellular localizations of these two enzymes
have not been experimentally determined, they are predicted
to localize to the ER owing to the presence of a signal
peptide (https://www.genscript.com/psort.html). Thus, iPRTP/
iPRDP/iPRMP are thought to be transported from the plastids
to the ER for the synthesis of tZ-type cytokinins by the enzymes CYP735A1/A2 (Takei et al., 2004a). Alternatively,
minor tZ-type cytokinins can be directly synthesized via the
IPT enzyme independent of iP-type cytokinins from an unknown precursor (A˚ stot et al., 2000).

The biosynthesis of DZ is still poorly understood. Enzyme assays
using crude enzymes from plants have suggested that DZ can be
formed by zeatin reductase, which reduces the N6
-side-chain
double bond of tZ or its metabolites (Gaudinova´ et al., 2005).
However, genes encoding zeatin reductase have yet to be
characterized.
Biosynthesis of free cytokinins in the cytoplasm and
apoplast

It has long been known that iP, tZ, and cZ nucleotides in the plastids and ER are transported to the cytoplasm and catalyzed by
LOG to produce free bases of iP, tZ, and cZ in a single step
(Kurakawa et al., 2007; Kuroha et al., 2009; Tokunaga et al.,
2011). iP and tZ nucleotides can be converted to free-type
cytokinins by dephosphorylation and deribosylation processes
(Chen and Kristopeit, 1981a, 1981b). Recently, the LOG family

Cytokinin/purine riboside nucleosidase 1,

As genes whose encoded enzymes function in cytokinin activation, the LOG genes are expressed in the shoot and root meristems. For example, in Arabidopsis, AtLOG1, AtLOG2, AtLOG4,

rice, OsLOG, OsLOGL3, and OsLOGL7 are expressed in

Biosynthesis of cytokinin species in shoots and roots
Transcripts of IPT genes have been detected in the shoots and
roots of plants such as Arabidopsis, rice, soybean, and maize
(Miyawaki et al., 2004, 2006; Kamada-Nobusada et al., 2013;
Ghosh et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2021). In Arabidopsis, AtIPT2,
AtIPT3, AtIPT5, AtIPT7, and AtIPT9 are expressed in the leaves
and roots; AtIPT4, AtIPT6, and AtIPT8 are expressed primarily
in flowers and seeds; and AtIPT1 is expressed in almost all
tissues (Miyawaki et al., 2004; Ghosh et al., 2018; Nguyen

et al., 2021). Among these, AtIPT3 and AtIPT7 are expressed in
the vascular tissues (Takei et al., 2004b; Miyawaki et al., 2004).
The expression patterns of IPT genes suggest that iP-type cytokinins can be produced in vascular tissues of both shoots and
roots. In contrast to the widely expressed IPTs, CYP735A2, the
major gene for tZ-type cytokinin biosynthesis in Arabidopsis, is
mainly expressed in vascular tissues of roots (Takei et al.,
2004a; Kiba et al., 2013). Similarly, in rice, the tZ-synthesis
genes CYP735A4 and CYP735A3 display higher expression in
roots than in shoots (Kiba et al., 2023). The expression
pattern of the tZ-biosynthesis gene CYP735A indicates that
tZ-type cytokinins are produced primarily in roots. At the
metabolic level, quantification of cytokinin species by liquid
chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry in grafts between
ipt1ipt3ipt5ipt7 quadruple mutants and wild-type plants suggests
that iP-type cytokinins are mainly produced in shoots, whereas
tZ-type cytokinins are mainly produced in roots (MatsumotoKitano et al., 2008). This suggests that iP-type cytokinins may
need to move from shoots to roots for the biosynthesis of tZtype cytokinins.
cZ-type cytokinin content varies greatly among different developmental stages of different plants. In Arabidopsis, the content of
cZ-type cytokinins in seeds was about three times that of tZtype cytokinins 24 h after seed soaking (Gajdosova´ et al.,
2011) but was about 10% that of tZ-type cytokinins in plants at
24 days after germination (Gajdosova´ et al., 2011). In rice, cZtype cytokinin content at the seedling stage was about 30 times
that of total tZ-type and iP-type cytokinins (Kiba et al., 2023),

but there was no obvious difference between cZ-type and tZtype cytokinin content after the tillering stage (Zhao et al., 2019;
Zhang et al., 2021). Interestingly, cZ and its derivatives are the
main cytokinin species in some Poaceae plants such as Avena
sativa, Triticum aestivum, Dactylis glomerata, Agropyron
repens, and Phragmites australis (Gajdosova´ et al., 2011).
Although the biosynthesis sites of cZ-type cytokinins remain
largely unknown, the available metabolic data show that there
is little difference in cZ content between shoots and roots
(Zhang et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2020), suggesting that cZ-type
cytokinins can be synthesized in both the roots and the shoots.
Compared with that of tZ-, iP-, and cZ-type cytokinins, the
content of DZ-type cytokinins is generally low in various plants
(Gajdosova´ et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Yin
et al., 2020), and little is known about their biosynthesis and
distribution.
The spatial distributions of different cytokinin species were
elegantly characterized by metabolic analysis of roots at
the single-cell level (Antoniadi et al., 2015). The cytokinin
concentration in root cells was approximately 3 3 1021 to 100 3
1021 pmol/cell (Antoniadi et al., 2015), with the highest levels
observed in distal root parts (root cap, columella, columella
initials, and quiescent center), followed by the endodermis and
the stele, and the lowest levels observed in cells of the cortex/
epidermis (Antoniadi et al., 2015). The cytokinins in roots are
mainly synthesized in the companion cells of the phloem and are
distributed to different tissues, indicating a clear phenomenon of
cytokinin transport in roots.
Conjugation and catabolism of cytokinins in multiple
organelles and in different tissues

After biosynthesis, cytokinins undergo glycosylation via glycosyltransferases or are irreversibly degraded by cytokinin oxidases
(Fox et al., 1973; Letham et al., 1983; Mok, 1994; Bilyeu et al.,
2001; Galuszka et al., 2001; Werner et al., 2001; Ashikari et al.,
2005). Cytokinin free bases are converted into cytokinin
ribosides by cytokinin riboside phosphorylase in the presence
of ribose 1-phosphate (Chen and Petschow, 1978; Bromley
et al., 2014) and can then be integrated into the metabolic
flux for synthesis of different cytokinin species. Cytokinin
glucosides are widely distributed in plants (Fox et al., 1973;
Letham et al., 1983; Dixon et al., 1989; Martin et al., 1999a,
1999b, 2001; Hou et al., 2004). After feeding of free 14C-labeled
tZ to Arabidopsis roots, various cytokinin species were
detected, including tZ, tZR, tZRMP, tZOG, tZROG, tZ7G, and
tZ9G (Zhang et al., 2014), suggesting that free tZ can be either
reversibly converted to tZR and tZRMP or glycosylated.
Cytokinin O-glucosyltransferases, which belong to the large
superfamily of glycosyltransferase enzymes, can catalyze N- or
O-glucosylation of cytokinins (Campbell et al., 1997; Lairson
et al., 2008; Yonekura-Sakakibara and Hanada, 2011).
In Arabidopsis, rice, and maize, cZ-O-glucosyltransferases
(cZOGT), including ZmcZOGT1, OscZOGT1, OscZOGT2,
OscZOGT3, and AtUGT85A1, catalyze O-glucosylation of
cytokinin free bases (Martin et al., 2001; Veach et al., 2003; Hou

et al., 2004; Kudo et al., 2012; Za´ veska´ Dra´ bkova´ et al., 2021).
In lima beans (Phaseolus lunatus), zeatin O-glucosyltransferase
1 and zeatin O-xylosyltransferase 1 catalyze O-glucosylation
and O-xylosylation of tZ (Dixon et al., 1989; Martin 1999a,
1999b). In maize, cytokinin O-glucosides were shown to be
reversibly deglycosylated by b-glucosidase (Brzobohaty et al.,
1993). Formation of glucosyl conjugates at the N3
, N7, and N9
positions of cytokinins is catalyzed by N-glucosyltransferases
(Entsch et al., 1979; Hou et al., 2004; Li et al., 2019). In
Arabidopsis and rice, glucosylation occurs at either the N7 or
the N9 position of cytokinins, but not at the N3 position, with
higher specific enzyme activity toward the N7 position of most
cytokinins (Hou et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2011; Li et al., 2019).
ZOGT, cZOGT, and N-glucosyltransferases were predicted
to localize primarily to the chloroplasts and cytoplasm in wheat
(T. aestivum) (Chen et al., 2021). On the other hand, N- and Oglucosyltransferase genes are expressed in both reproductive

CKX degrades cytokinins by catalyzing the irreversible conversion of cytokinins to adenine (Mok, 1994; Bilyeu et al., 2001;

Galuszka et al., 2001; Werner et al., 2001; Ashikari et al., 2005).
Mutations in CKX can increase cytokinin content in plants and
regulate plant development (Ashikari et al., 2005; Bartrina et al.,
2011; Gao et al., 2014, 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Huang et al.,
2023). CKX gene family members display various expression
patterns, subcellular localizations, and substrate preferences
and play multiple roles in planta. AtCKX3 and AtCKX5 are
nearly constitutively expressed, with their encoded proteins
localizing to the vacuole or the ER (Werner et al., 2003).
Mutations of AtCKX3/5 lead to an increase in endogenous
cytokinins, resulting in a 55% increase in seed yield (Bartrina
et al., 2011). AtCKX7 is expressed in the vascular tissue of
seedlings and in the female gametophyte (Kollmer et al., 2014 € ).
AtCKX7 has been shown to prefer cZ-type cytokinins (cZ and
cZ9G) and iP9G (Galuszka et al., 2001; Kollmer et al., 2014 € ).
Transgenic plants overexpressing AtCKX7 developed short,
early-terminating primary roots with smaller apical meristems
(Kollmer et al., 2014 € ). AtCKX1, AtCKX4, and AtCKX6 localize to
the ER (Werner et al., 2003; Niemann et al., 2018), AtCKX2 to
the apoplast (Werner et al., 2003), and AtCKX7 to the cytosol
(Kollmer et al., 2014 € ). AtCKX1 is mainly expressed in the roots
and hypocotyl, AtCKX2 in the flowers and seeds, and AtCKX6
in the roots, stem, and petiole (Werner et al., 2003). At the

biochemical level, AtCKX1 and AtCKX2 have been shown to prefer tZ-type cytokinins (Galuszka et al., 2001; Werner et al., 2001;
Kollmer et al., 2014 € ), and the enzyme activities of AtCKX1,
AtCKX2, and AtCKX4 toward iP cytokinin substrates are higher
than that of AtCKX3 (Werner et al., 2003).
In rice, the Gn1a (Grain number 1a) locus, a major quantitative
trait locus for increasing grain number, harbors a mutation in
OsCKX2 (Ashikari et al., 2005; Li et al., 2013; Tsago et al., 2020;
Tu et al., 2022). Knockdown of OsCKX2 in rice reduces yield
penalties under conditions of salinity stress (Joshi et al., 2018).
The highest OsCKX3 expression was observed in the rice
lamina joint, and the OsCKX3 protein localizes to the ER
(Huang et al., 2023). The osckx3 mutant displays a smaller leaf
angle and greater primary branch number, grain size, 1000-
grain weight, and flag-leaf size (Huang et al., 2023). OsCKX4 is
predominantly expressed in leaf blades and roots, and its
encoded protein localizes to the cytosol (Gao et al., 2014,
2019). OsCKX4 plays a positive role in crown root formation
and Zn uptake (Gao et al., 2014, 2019). Overexpression of
OsCKX5 results in increased uptake of certain macro- and
micronutrients, greater root biomass, and a deeper root system
(do Nascimento et al., 2021). OsCKX9 is highly expressed
in shoot bases, and its encoded protein localizes predominantly
to the cytosol and nuclei (Duan et al., 2019). osckx9
mutants and OsCKX9-overexpressing transgenic plants
showed significant increases in tiller number (Duan et al., 2019).
OsCKX9 is also involved in the regulation of leaf angle (Zhu

et al., 2024). OsCKX11 localizes to the cytosol, and the osckx11
mutation results in increased cytokinin content, delayed leaf
senescence, and enhanced panicle size (Zhang et al., 2021).
Collectively, mutations in OsCKX genes result in increased
cytokinin levels in specific tissues and positive regulation of
yield traits, suggesting that cytokinins have great potential for
application in crop molecular breeding.
Although the biosynthesis and metabolism of isoprene cytokinins
have been well studied, the enzymes involved in the biosynthesis
of aromatic cytokinins have not. Given that the processes of
cytokinin biosynthesis, conjugation, and degradation occur in
different organelles, cells, tissues, and organs, a significant number of transporters are required to regulate the spatial distribution
of cytokinin species.
CYTOKININ SIGNALING
Receptors of cytokinins in the PM and the ER
In Arabidopsis, three His kinases (Arabidopsis His kinase [AHK] 2,
AHK3, and CRE1/AHK4), all of which contain a cyclin His kinaseassociated sensory (CHASE) domain, an HK domain, and a
receiver domain, are characterized as cytokinin receptors
(Anantharaman and Aravind 2001; Ueguchi et al., 2001a,
2001b; Inoue et al., 2001; Mougel and Zhulin 2001; Suzuki
et al., 2001; Yamada et al., 2001; Hwang et al., 2002).
Differences in ligand preferences and expression patterns of
these receptors can lead to different strengths in signal
transmission. CRE1/AHK4 showed a high affinity for both iP
and tZ (Yamada et al., 2001; Romanov et al., 2006; Stolz et al.,
2011). The ligand-binding properties of AHK2 were shown to be
similar to those of CRE1/AHK4 (Stolz et al., 2011). By contrast,

cytokinin receptors are regulated at the transcriptional and
post-transcriptional levels to influence cytokinin signal output
and crop yield (Chun et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).
The subcellular localization of cytokinin receptors and where they
precisely interact with cytokinins remain controversial. Early experiments using GFP fusion proteins showed that the cytokinin
receptors of Arabidopsis and maize localized primarily to the
ER membrane (Caesar et al., 2011; Lomin et al., 2011;
Wulfetange et al., 2011). Although no clear evidence supports
localization of cytokinin receptors to the PM, the localization of
a minor but functionally relevant portion of the receptor pool at
the PM cannot be excluded (Lomin et al., 2011; Wulfetange
et al., 2011; Antoniadi et al., 2020). The activity of cytokinin
receptors depends on pH, with their hormone-binding activity being higher at pH 7–9 than at pH 5–7. Whereas the pH of the apoplast is usually between 4.5 and 6.0, the pH in the ER is 7–8, suggesting an intracellular function for cytokinin receptors (Romanov
et al., 2018). Interestingly, a study on the cytokinin transporter
purine permease (PUP) 14 revealed that removal of cytokinins
from the apoplast is essential for embryonic development,

activating cytokinin receptors (Zurcher et al., 2016a € ). Recently,

The transcriptional response to cytokinins is mainly mediated by
the RR family (D’Agostino et al., 2000; Hwang et al., 2001; Sakai

et al., 2001; Muller and Sheen, 2007; Muller, 2011). Type-B RRs
act as positive regulators of the cytokinin response, possessing

negative regulators of cytokinins, likely by competing with type-B

(Hwang and Sheen, 2001; Sakai et al., 2001; Nair et al., 2004).
However, the type-B RRs are not regulated by cytokinins at the
transcriptional level but rather at the post-transcriptional level
(Kieber and Schaller, 2014).

CYTOKININ TRANSPORT
The spatial expression patterns of genes involved in cytokinin
metabolism and signaling suggest that cytokinins can be synthesized locally, acting as autocrine or paracrine signals, or transported away from their sites of synthesis to exert biological functions. In the past decade, the characterization of transporters
involved in long-distance, intercellular, and intracellular cytokinin
transport, along with their underlying transport mechanisms, has
advanced significantly (Ko et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014, 2023;
Zurcher et al., 2016 € ; Xiao et al., 2019, 2020; Zhao et al., 2019,
2021, 2023; Tessi et al., 2021, 2023; Hu et al., 2023).
Transporters such as ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters,
PUPs, AZA-GUANINE RESISTANT (AZG) transporters, and equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENTs) have been characterized
for their roles involved in long-distance or local transport of cytokinins, thereby mediating hormone homeostasis during plant
development and stress responses (Figure 3).
Long-distance transport of cytokinins
The long-distance transport of tZ- and iP-type cytokinins is well
established in planta. Transcriptional analyses of cytokinin
biosynthesis genes, hormone profiling, and grafting experiments
have revealed that iP-type cytokinins are the predominant cytokinin species in shoots, whereas tZ-type cytokinins dominate in
roots (Hirose et al., 2008; Matsumoto-Kitano et al., 2008; Kiba
et al., 2013). Shoot-derived cytokinins move from shoots to roots
via the phloem, whereas root-derived cytokinins move from roots

to shoots via the xylem (Hirose et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).
Bidirectional transport of tZ- and iP-type cytokinins facilitates
the transduction of environmental cues from roots to shoots or
vice versa. Characterizing the mechanisms of long-distance
transport is crucial for understanding plant growth responses to
environmental changes.
In 2014, two independent studies identified Arabidopsis ABC
transporter subfamily G14 (AtABCG14) as a crucial PMlocalized transporter involved in the long-distance transport of
cytokinins from roots to shoots (Ko et al., 2014; Zhang et al.,
2014). In addition to its expression in the root stele, including
the pericycle, phloem, and xylem, AtABCG14 is widely
expressed in young tissues of the shoot. Histochemical GUS
staining revealed the expression of AtABCG14 in the phloem
and xylem region of the leaf midrib (Zhang et al., 2014; Zhao
et al., 2021). More recent studies using grafts between
atabcg14 and wild-type plants showed that AtABCG14 is

Experiments using split-root systems have demonstrated that

a potential circular transport mechanism within the vascular system of Arabidopsis (Zhao et al., 2021, 2023). This cyclic

has been identified as a key transporter responsible for tZ shootward transport (Zhao et al., 2019), suggesting a conserved

plants. In Medicago truncatula, MtABCG56 has been identified
as an exporter of bioactive cytokinins across the PM in an ATPdependent manner, and it is associated with nodulation
(Jarzyniak et al., 2021). However, the precise mechanism of
cytokinin transport mediated by these transporters in M.
truncatula remains to be clarified.
Intercellular and intracellular transport of cytokinins
PUPs are a family of energy-dependent and H+-coupled transporters with a high affinity for purine. Although initially identified
for their role in purine transport, some members of the PUP family
have been found to exhibit cytokinin transporter activity in vitro
and in vivo. Arabidopsis PUP1 and PUP2 exhibit cytokinin import

activities in yeast, although their physiological roles in plant
growth and development have not been fully characterized
(Gillissen et al., 2000; Burkle et al., 2003 € ). In 2016, Arabidopsis
PUP14 was biochemically and physiologically characterized as
a cytokinin influx transporter that plays essential roles in plant
development (Zurcher et al., 2016 € ). PUP14 is expressed from
the embryonic stage to the adult stage, and its encoded protein
localizes to the PM, where it imports bioactive cytokinins
such as tZ and iP from the apoplast to regulate cytokinin
homeostasis in the apoplast (Zurcher et al., 2016 € ). Interestingly,
our studies have shown that AtABCG14 is also localized to the
PM and functions in exporting cytokinins to the apoplast (Zhao
et al., 2021, 2023). This suggests that AtABCG14 and PUP14
may work synergistically to maintain cytokinin homeostasis in
the apoplast of plant cells. AtABCG14 likely functions in the intercellular transport of cytokinins, exporting them from the cell to the
apoplast, whereas PUP14 facilitates the import of cytokinins from
the apoplast into the cell. Together, these transporters contribute
to the regulation of cytokinin levels and signaling in plant tissues,
playing crucial roles in various aspects of plant growth and
development.
Recent research has shed light on the roles of specific PUPs in
the transport of cytokinins in plants. In Arabidopsis, PUP8 has
been identified as the PM-localized transporter responsible for
exporting cytokinins, whereas PUP7 and PUP21 localize to the
vacuole, where they facilitate the import of cytokinins (Hu et al.,
2023). Their triple mutants (CRISPR7/8/21) exhibit a dwarf
phenotype and reduced cytoplasmic cytokinin levels compared
with the wild type (Hu et al., 2023), indicating the importance of
these transporters for cytokinin homeostasis and regulation of
plant growth. In rice, OsPUP1 has been found to localize to the
ER and functions as a cytokinin importer, potentially unloading

cytokinins from the vascular tissues transported through the
symplastic pathway and thereby affecting root-to-shoot longdistance transport of cytokinins (Xiao et al., 2020). Furthermore,
OsPUP4 and OsPUP7 were discovered to work sequentially,
with OsPUP4 transporting hormones from the apoplast into the
cytoplasm and OsPUP7 transporting them into the ER lumen
for further cell-to-cell transport, thereby affecting both long-distance movement and local allocation of cytokinins (Xiao et al.,
2019). Moreover, in Arabidopsis, ABCI19, ABCI20, and ABCI21
have been identified as ER-localized cytokinin transporters expressed in young seedlings. These proteins form a large protein
complex at the ER membrane and are involved in the intercellular
transport of cytokinins, affecting cytokinin homeostasis near
cytokinin receptors. Mutations in abci19, abci20, and abci21
compromise the response to cytokinin treatments in seedlings,
further highlighting the importance of ER-localized cytokinin
transporters for cytokinin signaling and response (Kim et al.,
2020). These findings contribute to our understanding of the
complex mechanisms involved in cytokinin transport and
signaling in plants.
Recent research has highlighted the role of AZG transporters in
the intercellular and intracellular transport of cytokinins (Tessi
et al., 2021, 2023). AZG2, a purine transporter, has been found
to be expressed in a specific group of cells surrounding
LR primordia, with its expression induced by auxins (Tessi
et al., 2021). It localizes to the ER and the PM, suggesting its
involvement in transport of cytokinins from the PM to the ER.
Biochemical analyses have revealed that AZG2 exhibits strong
influx transport activity toward various cytokinins, including iP,
tZ, benzyladenine (BA), and kinetin, in addition to adenine. The
azg2 mutant is partially insensitive to exogenous cytokinins and
has higher LR density, indicating the role of AZG2 in regulating
cytokinin homeostasis in cells surrounding the root primordia.

REGULATION OF THE SPATIAL
DISTRIBUTIONS OF CYTOKININS
Cytokinins play crucial roles as important signaling molecules
that facilitate long-distance communication between organs,
thereby contributing to systemic regulation of growth in response
to environmental changes in plants (Sakakibara, 2021). Cytokinin
transport between shoots and roots coordinates plant growth
with environmental cues. Root-derived cytokinins, including
free tZ and tZR, are transported via the xylem and regulate leaf
growth and meristem size, whereas shoot-derived cytokinins,
including iP and iPR, are transported via the phloem and influence
root growth or nodulation (Muraro et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2014;
Sasaki et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Osugi et al., 2017).
Environmental factors and internal cues modulate plant
development and stress responses by dynamically adjusting
the spatial distributions of cytokinins.
The regulation of plant growth via spatial distributions of cytokinins under different carbon and nitrogen (N) conditions is summarized in Figure 4. N is an important factor that influences plant
growth rate and final biomass. In Arabidopsis, expression levels
of the cytokinin biosynthesis genes IPT3 and CYP735A2
increase substantially upon N application (Takei et al., 2004b;

Maeda et al., 2018). The atabcg14 mutant exhibits a
suppressed response to N starvation, highlighting the essential
role of long-distance cytokinin transport in N signaling (Poitout
et al., 2018). Exogenous application of cytokinins represses the
expression of a subset of root-type nitrate transporters, including
NRT2.1 and NRT2.3, which are major high-affinity nitrate transporters (Kiba et al., 2010). In addition, cytokinin biosynthesis is
upregulated under high-N conditions compared with low-N conditions (Kiba et al., 2010). The small peptides C-TERMINALLY

Carbon derived from photosynthesis is a key regulator of plant
growth and development. Kiba et al. reported that sugarinduced cytokinin biosynthesis and transport play roles in growth
enhancement under elevated CO2 in Arabidopsis (Kiba et al.,

in roots were induced by CO2 or sugars but were inhibited by

Abiotic stresses such as salt and variations in photoperiod have a
significant impact on the spatial distributions of cytokinins,

thereby regulating plant growth and stress responses. Yin et al.
reported that Argonaute2 (AGO2) enhances grain length and
salt tolerance by activating expression of BIG GRAIN3 (BG3)/
OsPUP4 to modulate cytokinin distributions in rice (Yin et al.,
2020). AGO2 can be enriched on the BG3 locus and alter its
histone methylation level, thus promoting BG3 expression. Both
AGO2 and BG3 are transcriptionally suppressed by salt
treatment. Salt treatment markedly increases cytokinin levels in
roots but decreases them in shoots, resulting in a hormone
distribution pattern similar to that of AGO2-overexpressing
plants. OsPUP7 and OsABCG18 are also significantly suppressed by salt stress, suggesting their involvement in cytokinin
distribution between roots and shoots under salt stress. Thus,
in response to high external salinity, plants adjust their internal
cytokinin distributions to enhance their tolerance to stress.
Consistent with this scenario, transient induction of IPT in the
roots of tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) via HSP70::IPT has
been shown to result in increased cytokinin levels in shoots,
improving shoot growth and fruit yield under salinized conditions
(Ghanem et al., 2010). Frank and Cortleven found that
photoperiod stress increases cytokinin content and suppresses
lesions and photosynthetic capacity in leaves (Frank and
Cortleven, 2020). They proposed that photoperiod stress
induces the expression of IPT and CYP735A proteins to
increase synthesis of tZ-type cytokinins in the roots, which are
then transported via AtABCG14 to the shoots, where they activate cytokinin signaling and the stress response.
Regulation of transporters at the post-transcriptional or protein
level can directly influence cytokinin transport and shape the
spatial distributions of cytokinins in plants. PUP transporters
import substrates through proton co-transport mechanisms.
The importance of energizing cytokinin transport has been
demonstrated with the help of a protonophore that collapses proton gradients across membranes, thereby inhibiting active transmembrane transport (Cedzich et al., 2008). Application of a
protonophore has been shown to affect the accumulation of

cytokinins in root cells, their distributions between roots and
shoots, their concentrations in xylem sap, and their rates of
delivery to shoots of durum wheat (Triticum turgidum) in the
presence and absence of exogenous zeatin at the roots
(Kudoyarova et al., 2014). This suggests that interacting protein
partners or co-transporters may also regulate transporter activity.
FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
Cytokinin receptors have been found to localize to the ER and the
PM, which sense intracellular and apoplastic cytokinins, respectively. However, the mechanisms by which different cytokinin
species are delivered to the receptors via the apoplastic or symplastic pathway have yet to be clearly characterized. Moreover,
the differences between signal relays from ER- and PMlocalized receptors remain unknown. Although cytokinin signal
transduction has been well characterized through the binary
two-component system, it is unclear how various type-A and
type-B ARR proteins function with cytokinins in specific physiological roles. Various cytokinin species, including iP, tZ, and cZ,
possess different binding affinities for cytokinin receptors
(Yonekura-Sakakibara et al., 2004; Romanov et al., 2006; Lomin
et al., 2011), and the functions of these different types of
cytokinin within specific signaling pathways remain to be
determined.
The long-distance transport of cytokinins by AtABCG14 between
roots and shoots has been well described, but several key steps
in the process require further characterization, including: (1) how
root-derived cytokinins are transmitted from xylem to phloem for
distribution during root-to-shoot transport, (2) how shootsynthesized cytokinins are loaded into phloem for shoot-to-root
transport, and (3) how the iP-type cytokinins in phloem are unloaded to the tZ-biosynthesizing cells for tZ synthesis. With regard to the intercellular and intracellular transport of cytokinins,
the transporters involved in intracellular transport, such as those
involved in efflux transport of cytokinin nucleotides from plastids,
need further identification. The mechanisms by which cytokinin

sugar conjugates are transported to vacuoles also require investigation. Shoot and root meristem activities are both under the
control of cytokinins, but the cellular transport of cytokinins in apical meristem cells and its regulation remain to be clarified. In
addition to the apoplastic transport pathway, the symplastic
pathway plays an essential role in cytokinin transport, although
this transport mechanism is not well characterized.

involved in the regulation of cytokinin distributions in rice roots
and shoots under salt stress (Yin et al., 2020). However, the
transcriptional and post-translational regulation of other cytokinin
transporters remains largely unknown. Characterizing the regulators or protein interaction partners of these transporters at the
molecular level will provide a deeper understanding of the regulatory network for cytokinin distribution and signaling. These
